title: Breaking the Curse of Dimensionality in Quantum PDE Solvers via Gevrey Regularity
authors: Pooya Ronagh, Mariia Sobchuk, Xiaoran Li, Arsalan Motamedi, Grecia Castelazo, Ala Shayeghi
abstract: We connect different degrees of smoothness of real-valued periodic functions to the cost of preparing their high-precision Fourier-basis amplitude encodings as quantum states. Our central observation is that the Gevrey hierarchy, which stratifies the space between smooth and analytic functions, provides a natural class for high-precision quantum algorithms. We then specialize to solving general linear partial differential equations (PDEs), showing how our Fourier methods do so efficiently at varying target precisions on a quantum computer. This also demonstrates how our framework enables passage from query-complexity results to explicit elementary gate counts. As an application, we introduce a hierarchy of many-body quantum simulation pipelines that harness these high-precision algorithms to probe the linear response of atomistic systems in first quantization. Each level of the hierarchy unlocks a further polynomial-degree quantum speedup, yielding a gradual improvement in simulation efficiency as quantum computers scale.
summary: This paper develops a theoretical framework showing that by leveraging the mathematical concept of Gevrey regularity, one can efficiently solve high-dimensional linear Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) on a quantum computer. This approach overcomes classical scaling limitations and provides a pathway to achieving polynomial quantum speedups for simulating complex many-body systems in condensed matter physics.
main_problem: The core problem is overcoming the 'Curse of Dimensionality' when using quantum algorithms to solve high-precision Partial Differential Equations (PDEs).
main_result: The authors establish a framework showing that utilizing Gevrey regularity allows for efficient, polynomial-degree quantum speedups in solving linear PDEs at varying target precisions.
method: They connect function smoothness (via the Gevrey hierarchy) to the cost of preparing high-precision Fourier-basis amplitude encodings and apply this to solve discretized linear PDE systems using QLSA techniques.
model_or_system: The methods are applied to general linear PDEs, including those arising in many-body quantum simulations (like the Sternheimer equation derived from DFT) for probing atomistic systems.
key_observables: Linear response observables such as density response ($\deltaho$), induced potentials ($\delta V_H$, $\delta V_{xc}$), and general correlation functions.
important_parameters: Target precision ($\epsilon$), Gevrey smoothness parameter ($s$), cutoff mode ($N$), and the dimensionality of the problem ($d$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies heavily on assuming $s$-Gevrey regularity for the solutions to guarantee polynomial scaling in dimension, and it requires using a closure approximation when extending to higher-order correlation functions.
figures_summary: Table I compares classical vs. quantum complexity bounds for solving PDEs; Table II relates quantum hardness to function smoothness classes via Fourier coefficient decay rates.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the theoretical link between Gevrey regularity and quantum encoding costs, then specializes this framework to solve general linear PDEs using Fourier methods, and finally applies this machinery to build a hierarchy of many-body simulation pipelines for atomistic systems.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses how mathematical properties (smoothness) dictate the feasibility and scaling of quantum computation for fundamental physics problems like electronic structure calculations. The explicit link between Gevrey classes and polynomial speedup is highly relevant to designing practical quantum algorithms for condensed matter theory.
